analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from collecting or selling personal reproductive and sexual health data without written consent.
analysis.headline: A bill to bar companies from collecting or selling personal reproductive and sexual health data died in committee without ever receiving a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped companies from gathering, keeping, using, or selling personal reproductive or sexual health information — including details about pregnancies, contraception, fertility, and location data that might reveal a trip to a clinic — unless the person gave express written consent or the data was strictly needed to provide a requested service. It would have let people see and delete their data, required companies to publish privacy policies, and let both the FTC and individuals enforce the rules. It never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses period trackers, fertility apps, pharmacy delivery, or search engines while seeking reproductive or sexual health care. The bill would have required written consent before companies could collect or share that data, given people the right to see and delete it, and made it easier to sue companies that violate the rules. The people most protected would be women in states that restrict abortion, where digital trails could be used as evidence.

how_it_helps.text: Bars commercial entities from collecting, keeping, using, or selling personal reproductive or sexual health data unless the person gave express written consent or it is strictly necessary to provide the service they asked for.
Gives individuals the right to see what data a company holds about them — including data bought from brokers and inferred by algorithms — and to have it deleted within 15 days at no charge.
Lets the FTC enforce the rules, and lets individuals sue violators for damages, with attorney's fees available and mandatory arbitration clauses unenforceable for these disputes.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from collecting and selling health and location data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app makers outside HIPAA coverage — would lose a source of sellable data and face compliance and litigation costs.

drawbacks.text: The definition of covered information is very broad, covering everything from pregnancy status to location data that 'might indicate' someone sought reproductive services, and its broad reach could be legally contested or create compliance uncertainty.
Private lawsuits can seek up to $1,000 per violation per day plus punitive damages, and companies handling any adjacent data face potentially large litigation exposure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and specific: after abortion became illegal or restricted in many states, the app and search trail left by anyone seeking reproductive care could be used against them, and no other federal law filled that gap. The costs are modest compliance burdens on companies handling this data, and the main honest objection is definitional breadth and liability risk. On balance, a well-designed consumer privacy measure whose death was the product of inaction, not a fair vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 16, 2022 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with no committee vote and no floor vote in either chamber.

The bill would have required express written consent before companies could collect, retain, use, or disclose personal reproductive or sexual health information, including data about pregnancies, contraception, and location signals that might indicate someone sought such services.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app makers can continue collecting and monetizing reproductive health data.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and health-data app makers

for.name: Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: 12 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Wyden, Gillibrand, Klobuchar, and Booker

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, allowing it to expire at the end of the 117th Congress without a hearing or vote.

against.name: Tech industry and data broker firms
against.what_they_did: Companies that profit from health and location data generally oppose strict consent requirements and private rights of action in privacy legislation.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee calendar never advanced it.

industries.note: They could no longer buy, sell, or infer reproductive health data — including location data suggesting someone visited a clinic — without written consent, cutting off a lucrative data category. The public interest in not being tracked this way runs directly against their business model.

industries.industry: Period and fertility tracking app makers
industries.note: Apps outside HIPAA would face new consent, deletion, and disclosure requirements, limiting how they monetize user data. Their users gain strong privacy protections.

The bill exempts entities already subject to HIPAA privacy rules, leaving the existing medical privacy regime as the sole channel for regulated health data while the unregulated app-and-broker ecosystem gets new rules.
